title: Plants are alive: parts, light and slow movement
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Biology: plant parts (Unit 2.1) and plants and light (Unit 2.3), and goes wider: roots growing down, stems as water pipes, which parts we eat, and plants that move slowly. No textbook needed.
summary: Your child meets plants as living things that do things: they drink through their roots, carry water up their stems like pipes, cook their own food in their leaves, and move, very slowly, towards light and down towards the Earth. They take a plant apart, grow a bean through a shoebox maze, watch coloured water climb a stem, turn a jar of seeds upside down to see roots turn round, and find that a plant always finds the light.
builds_on: This is the first rung. Seeds and how they sprout come in the Class 1 seeds rung. In Class 3 your child comes back to plants: kinds of plants, fair tests of what plants need, how water climbs a tall tree and how a tree is built mostly from air. The Plants Mission book goes deeper still.
goals: By the end your child can point to the root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed on real plants and say one job each part does.
By the end your child can explain that plants are alive: they grow, drink, make their own food and respond to light and to gravity.
By the end your child can show that a plant grows towards light and its roots grow down, and predict which way a plant on a windowsill will lean.
By the end your child can say that a plant kept in the dark goes pale, tall and weak, and why.
By the end your child can sort the vegetables in the kitchen by which part of the plant we eat.
By the end your child can care for a plant for two weeks and record what changes.
words: the part under the ground that holds the plant and drinks water
the part that holds the plant up and carries water, like a pipe
the green part that makes food from sunlight
the part that holds and protects the seeds
a baby plant with its packed lunch, waiting to grow
light from the Sun, which plants use to make food
the green stuff in leaves that catches sunlight
the pull of the Earth that makes things fall down; roots feel it and grow towards it
growing, needing food and water, and responding to the world
subconcepts: roots hold the plant and drink water
the stem holds the plant up and carries water like a pipe
leaves make the plant's food from sunlight, water and air (photosynthesis)
chlorophyll makes leaves green, and is made only in light
flowers make seeds; fruits hold and protect seeds
we eat roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds

days.title: Is it alive?
days.goal: Notice that plants are living things that do things.

steps.title: Alive or not?
steps.do: Put four things on the table: a stone, a potted plant (or a sprig of tulsi), a toy and a banana. Ask: 'Which of these are alive? How do you know?' Listen to the reasons. Then ask: 'Can the plant move? Can it eat?' Say: 'Let's find out. Plants do more than you think.'

steps.title: Plant walk
steps.do: Walk around your building or street for 15 minutes. Look for plants in surprising places: in cracks in walls, on roofs, in drains. Ask at each one: 'How did it get here? What is it drinking? Where is its food?' Collect one fallen leaf and one weed with its roots (from a crack, with permission).

steps.title: What do plants do?
steps.do: At home, lay out the weed. Ask: 'If this plant could talk, what would it say about living in a crack?' Write your child's words down. Ask: 'Who planted it? Nobody! So is it a weed, or a brave plant? Who decides?' (People call a plant a weed when it grows where they don't want it; to the bee or the ant it is just a plant.) Then tell your child about voice v2: an Indian scientist, J.C. Bose, showed plants react when they are hurt. Ask: 'Do you think the weed felt it when we pulled it up? How could we find out?'

need: a stone, a potted plant, a toy, a banana

days.title: Parts of a plant
days.goal: Find the root, stem, leaf and flower on real plants and say what each does.

steps.title: Plant body
steps.do: Make your body a plant: feet are roots holding the ground, legs and body are the stem standing up, arms are leaves spread to the sun, and your face is a flower. Say each part as you stretch.

steps.title: Take a plant apart
steps.do: Use the weed from Day 1 or a coriander plant from the market with roots on. Lay it on white paper. Your child finds and touches each part. Ask: 'What does the root feel like? Why is it so long and thin?' (To reach water and hold on tight; tug the plant gently and feel the soil holding it.) 'Why is the stem stiff?' (To hold the leaves up to the light.) 'Why is the leaf flat and wide?' (To catch lots of sunlight, like a solar panel.) If there is a flower or a seed pod, find it: 'The flower makes seeds. The fruit is the box that keeps them safe.' Sniff the leaves of coriander or mint. Then do Worksheet ws1.

steps.title: Plant printing
steps.do: Do Activity a1: paint a leaf and press it onto paper to make prints. Look for the veins in the print. Ask: 'What are these lines for?' (They carry water, like tiny pipes.)

need: a small plant with roots (weed or coriander)

days.title: Plants need light
days.goal: Start two experiments about light and plants.

steps.title: Window lean
steps.do: Look at a plant that lives near a window. Ask: 'Which way is it leaning? Why do you think?' Then turn the pot halfway round and say: 'Let's see what it does in a few days.'

steps.title: The shoebox maze
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: build a shoebox maze with one hole at the top and plant a sprouted bean at the bottom. This takes 1–2 weeks, so check it every two days.

steps.title: Light or dark?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: sow moong in two cups, one on the windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.

need: a sprouted bean or rajma (soak overnight)
moong, two cups with damp cotton

prep.task: Soak a few rajma or big beans overnight, then keep them in a damp cloth for a day until they sprout

days.title: Pipes in the stem, roots that go down
days.goal: See water climb a stem, and find out that roots always turn to grow down.

steps.title: Check the moong
steps.do: Peep at the two moong cups from Day 3. Ask: 'Which cup is growing faster? Which is greener?' Don't explain yet; just say: 'Keep watching. They are telling us something.'

steps.title: Coloured water climbs
steps.do: Do Experiment e3: stand a white flower (or a celery stick or a balsam stem) in a glass of water darkened with ink or food colour. Ask your child to guess: 'Will the colour stay in the glass, or go somewhere?' Mark the glass with the time. Say: 'Your blood travels round your body in tubes. A plant has tubes too. Let's see if we can catch the water moving.' You'll look again tomorrow.

steps.title: The upside-down jar
steps.do: Do Experiment e4: put 4 soaked rajma or chana seeds between wet paper towel and the side of a clear jar, so you can see them. Tell your child: 'When the roots are as long as your fingernail, we will turn the jar upside down. Then the roots will be pointing UP. What do you think they will do?' Write the guess on the jar with a marker.

steps.title: Up and down
steps.do: Ask: 'Shoots go up. Roots go down. Even in a dark cupboard, roots go down. How does a root know which way is down, with no eyes?' Drop a ball: 'What pulls the ball down?' (The Earth's pull: gravity.) Say: 'Roots can feel that pull, and they grow towards it. Shoots grow away from it.'

need: a white flower, celery or balsam stem
a glass, ink or food colour
a clear jar, paper towel, 4 soaked rajma or chana

prep.task: Soak 4 rajma or chana seeds overnight

days.title: How does a plant eat?
days.goal: Understand that leaves make food from sunlight, water and air.

steps.title: Where did the colour go?
steps.do: Look at the flower from Experiment e3. Ask: 'Where is the colour now?' (In the petals, in lines, or in the leaves.) With a grown-up's knife, cut the stem across and look at the cut end: 'See the coloured dots? Those are the pipes. The water climbed up them, all the way from the glass to the top.' Also measure the tallest moong sprout in each cup with a paper strip and stick the strips side by side in your notebook.

steps.title: The leaf kitchen
steps.do: Hold a leaf up to the light. Say: 'A leaf is a tiny kitchen. It takes water from the roots, through the pipes we just saw, and air from all around, and sunlight, and it cooks them into sugar, the plant's food. Scientists call this photosynthesis, which means making with light. The green stuff that catches the light is called chlorophyll. And while it cooks, the leaf breathes out the fresh air we breathe in.' Ask: 'So what would happen to a plant with no light?' (No cooking, so no food; and it can't make its green.) Ask: 'You get your food from the kitchen. Who makes all the food in the world, at the very start?' (Plants!)

steps.title: Play Sun, Water, Grow!
steps.do: Play the board game (g1). Each square is something that helps or harms a plant; your child says why before moving. On 'A goat nibbles you', ask: 'Is the goat bad? The goat is hungry too. Who makes the goat's food?'

need: the printed board game, a die and coins

days.title: Which part do we eat? And a plant friend
days.goal: Find out that we eat every part of a plant, and start caring for one plant.

steps.title: Maze and jar check
steps.do: Open the shoebox lid quickly and look at the bean. Ask: 'Which way is it growing? How does it know where the hole is?' Close it fast. Look at the jar from Experiment e4: if the roots are as long as a fingernail, turn the jar upside down now and put it back.

steps.title: The sabzi sort
steps.do: Do Activity a2: lay out vegetables and foods from the kitchen and sort them onto six papers labelled root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed. Surprises to talk about: a potato is a fat underground stem (it has 'eyes' that grow shoots); cauliflower is a bunch of flower buds; a tomato, bhindi and brinjal are fruits because they hold seeds; dal and rice are seeds. Ask: 'Which part did you eat most today?'

steps.title: Project: my plant friend
steps.do: Start the project: your child chooses a pot plant (or plants a tulsi or methi seedling), names it, measures it with a strip of paper, draws it, and sets up a care chart for two weeks with three columns: water, light, how it looks. Ask: 'What will your plant need from you every day? What does it get by itself?'

steps.title: Plants and light
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Read each question aloud and let your child answer from what they have seen in the experiments so far. For the written questions, your child says the answer and you write it.

need: potato, onion, carrot, spinach, cauliflower, tomato, bhindi, a few grains of rice and dal, a piece of sugarcane or celery if you have it

days.title: What did the plants do?
days.goal: Look at the results, think about big questions and teach it back.

steps.title: Results
steps.do: Compare the two moong cups (the dark ones are tall, thin and yellow; the light ones shorter and green), look at the window plant you turned on Day 3 (it has started leaning back towards the light), and look at the upside-down jar (the root tips have bent round to grow down again). Open the maze: has the bean found its way? Ask: 'Did the plant see the light? It has no eyes. How did it know? How did the root know which way was down?' Then put the dark cup on the windowsill: 'Watch it turn green in a day or two.'

steps.title: Big questions
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Tell it like a story: 'Two scientists, a father and his son, put tiny caps on the tips of grass shoots, and the shoots stopped bending to the light.' Ask the big question: 'Plants have no eyes, but they find the light. Which part of our maze bean was looking?' Then ask the challenge question: 'Are plants just still things, like furniture?' Show your child (or tell them about) a touch-me-not folding, or a tamarind or rain tree whose leaves fold up at dusk. 'They move. They are just slower than us.'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows a grown-up or a toy the parts of a plant, the moong cups and the maze, and explains what happened. Ask the check questions. Try Worksheet ws3's puzzles if they want more.

experiments.title: The shoebox maze
experiments.question: Can a plant find its way to the light?
need: two pieces of cardboard and tape
steps: Cut a hole about the size of a ₹10 coin in one short end of the box, near the top.
Tape two pieces of cardboard inside as shelves, one from the left and one from the right, to make a zigzag path.
Plant the sprouted bean in the cup and put it at the bottom of the box, far from the hole.
Close the lid and stand the box with the hole facing a sunny window.
Every two days, water the bean a little and close the lid again quickly.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the bean find the hole? Which way will it grow?'
experiments.observe: Draw the shoot each time you check.
experiments.why: Plants sense light with special proteins, mostly near their growing tips, and grow faster on the shaded side so they bend towards the light. The bean twists round the shelves until it reaches the hole.

experiments.title: Light or dark?
experiments.question: What happens to seedlings grown without light?
steps: Put 10 soaked moong on damp cotton in each cup.
Put one on a sunny windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.
Keep both damp.
After 4–5 days, compare them.
experiments.observe: Height and colour of the sprouts.
experiments.why: In the dark, seedlings use their stored food to grow tall and thin as fast as they can, searching for light, and they stay yellow because they make green chlorophyll only in light. In light they grow shorter, stronger and green.

experiments.title: Coloured water climbs the stem
experiments.question: How does water get from the bottom of a plant to the top?
need: a white flower (chrysanthemum, rose, white daisy), a celery stick or a balsam stem
steps: Half fill the glass with water and stir in plenty of colour.
A grown-up cuts the bottom of the stem at a slant.
Stand the stem in the coloured water and note the time.
Look after 1 hour, at bedtime and the next morning.
Next day, a grown-up cuts across the stem so your child can look at the cut end.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the colour stay in the glass? If it moves, where will it go?'
experiments.observe: Coloured lines in the petals or leaves, and coloured dots in the cut stem.
experiments.why: The stem has bundles of very thin tubes (called xylem) that carry water up from the roots. Water is pulled up them as the leaves and petals let water go into the air. The coloured dots in the cut stem are the ends of the tubes.
experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Food colour can stain, so use an old cloth.

experiments.title: The upside-down jar
experiments.question: Do roots always know which way is down?
need: 4 rajma or chana seeds soaked overnight
steps: Line the inside of the jar with folded paper towel.
Push 4 soaked seeds between the towel and the glass, halfway up, so you can see them.
Put 2 cm of water in the bottom so the towel stays wet.
When the roots are about 1 cm long (2–3 days), turn the jar upside down and stand it on its lid, or lay it on its side.
Look every day for 3 days and draw the roots.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When the roots point up, will they keep growing up?'
experiments.observe: Within a day or two, the root tips bend round and grow down again.
experiments.why: Root tips have special cells that feel which way gravity pulls, a bit like tiny heavy grains settling at the bottom of a bag. The root then grows more on its top side, so it curves down. Shoots do the opposite. Scientists call this gravitropism.

activities.title: Leaf prints
steps: Paint the back of a leaf, where the veins stand out.
Press it paint-side down on paper and rub gently.
Lift it off and look at the print.
Try three different leaves and compare their veins.
activities.outcome: A page of leaf prints showing the veins, the plant's water pipes.

activities.title: The sabzi sort
need: six sheets of paper labelled root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed
vegetables and foods from the kitchen
steps: Lay out the six papers.
Pick up each food and ask: 'Which part of the plant is this?'
Put it on the right paper. Cut one open if you need to look for seeds.
Talk about the surprises: potato (stem), cauliflower (flowers), tomato and bhindi (fruits), dal (seeds), carrot and mooli (roots), spinach (leaves).
activities.outcome: A table showing that we eat every part of a plant.

project.title: My plant friend
steps: Choose a plant and give it a name.
Measure it with a paper strip and draw it.
Make a care chart: water, light, how it looks.
Look after it for two weeks, measuring every few days.
Tell the family what your plant did.
project.outcome: A two-week plant diary with drawings and paper-strip measurements.

game.title: Sun, Water, Grow!
rules: Everyone starts as a seed on START.
Read the square aloud and say why it helps or harms a plant.
First plant to reach BLOOM wins.
squares: START: a seed in the soil
Kept in a dark cupboard: miss a turn
Too much water, roots soggy: back 1
Someone pulls you up as a weed: back 3
Hot dry day, no water: back 1

big: Plants have no eyes. How do they know where the light is?
Is a plant still, or is it moving very, very slowly?
Where does a plant's food come from? Where does ours come from?
Who decides whether a plant is a weed?
If you were a plant, what would you need most?

challenge.q: People say plants just sit there and don't do anything. Is that true?
challenge.hint: Look at the maze bean and the window plant. They moved, chose a direction and changed how they grew. They just do it slowly. If we filmed them and played it fast, they'd look busy!

challenge.q: Is a plant 'alive' in the same way you are?
challenge.hint: It grows, drinks, makes food, responds to light and makes babies (seeds). It can't walk or talk. Ask: does something need to move like us to be alive?

challenge.q: People say a plant gets its food from the soil, like we get food from a plate. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Soil gives water and a few minerals. The food itself, sugar, is made in the leaves from sunlight, water and air. That's why a plant in the dark starves even in good soil. Ask: what happened to our dark moong?

perspectives.who: A plant in a crack in the wall
perspectives.view: Nobody planted it, nobody waters it, and it still grows, using a little rain and sunlight. Ask: is it a weed, or is it brave?

perspectives.who: A grandmother who keeps a tulsi
perspectives.view: Many Indian families care for a tulsi every day, watering it and lighting a lamp near it. Ask: what do you think people learn from looking after one plant every day for years?
To a bee, a dandelion in a crack or a flower on a 'weed' is a meal. Ask: if bees named plants, which ones would they call weeds?

voices.who: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and his son Francis Darwin (1848–1925), England
voices.idea: In 1880 the Darwins grew grass seedlings in the dark and lit them from one side with a lamp so dim that they themselves could hardly see it. The seedlings still bent towards it. When they put tiny caps on just the tips, the seedlings stopped bending. So the very tip 'sees' the light, and tells the part lower down to bend.
voices.then: Many scientists doubted that a message could travel inside a plant without nerves.
voices.now: They were right. Scientists later found the message: a plant chemical called auxin. Plants have several light-sensing proteins, not eyes. And Francis did much of the work; his name is on the book, in smaller letters, 'assisted by Francis Darwin'.
voices.ask: Our maze bean found the hole. Which part of it do you think was 'looking' for the light?

voices.idea: Bose built very sensitive machines to show that plants respond to touch, heat and injury with tiny electrical signals, a bit like animals' nerves.
voices.then: Some scientists in Europe laughed at the idea that plants could 'feel'. He kept testing and published his results.
voices.now: Scientists today agree that plants send electrical signals through their bodies. Whether this is anything like feeling is still argued about.
voices.ask: If a plant reacts when it's hurt, does that mean it feels pain? What would we need to know to decide?

story.title: The Bean That Found the Window
text: Meera broke her leg on the last day of the summer holidays, jumping off the wall behind her building. The doctor put it in a heavy white plaster, and said she must keep it still for six weeks.

Six weeks! Meera's room was small, at the back of the flat, and it had only one tiny window, high up near the ceiling, where a square of sky showed through. All day the other children played in the lane below. Meera could hear them, but she couldn't see them. She lay in her bed and stared at the ceiling and felt as if she were at the bottom of a well.
On the third day, her Nani came to visit, carrying a shoebox.
"What's in it?" Meera asked, not very interested.

"A bean," said Nani. She opened the lid. Inside the box were little cardboard walls, like the walls of a maze, and at the very bottom, in a tiny cup of soil, was a fat rajma bean with a pale shoot just poking out of it. At the top of the box, at the far end, was a small round hole.

"The bean is at the bottom of a well, like you," said Nani. "It's dark down there. Let's see if it can find the light." She closed the lid, and put the box on the table under the little window, with the hole facing the light.
"It can't," said Meera. "It hasn't got eyes. It doesn't even know where the hole is."
"Hm," said Nani, which was what she always said when she disagreed but wanted you to find out for yourself.

Every two days, Meera's mother lifted the lid for one minute so Meera could peep in and give the bean a spoon of water. The first time, the shoot had grown up to the first cardboard wall and stopped. "See," said Meera. "It's stuck."

But the second time, the shoot had turned. It had bent sideways, along the underside of the wall, towards the gap at the end. The third time, it had found the gap and gone round it, and was climbing towards the second wall. It was pale and thin and determined, and it was going the right way.

Meera began to look forward to the peeps. She drew the shoot in her notebook every time, a little longer and a little twistier. "How does it know?" she kept asking. "It's dark in there. How does it know which way the light is?"

"Plants can feel light," said Nani. "Not with eyes. With their whole growing tip. They feel which side the light is coming from, even a tiny bit of light, and they grow faster on the dark side, so they bend towards the bright side. They never stop trying."

In the fifth week, Meera was allowed to sit up in a chair by the window, and then to hop to the balcony with crutches. She could see the lane again. She could see the other children. She waved, and they waved back and shouted that they had saved her a turn in hopscotch for when the plaster came off.
On the morning the plaster came off, Meera's leg was pale and thin and wobbly, and she had to learn to walk on it again, a little at a time. She went to the table and lifted the lid of the shoebox.

The bean had done it. Its long, twisty stem had wound all the way around both walls, and its two first leaves had pushed right out of the round hole at the top, into the sunlight. Outside the box, in the light, the leaves were green.
Meera looked at her own pale leg, and at the pale stem, and at the green leaves in the sun. Then she looked out of the window at the lane.
story.epiphany: Plants sense light without eyes (with light-sensing proteins near the growing tip) and grow towards it, even through a maze; without light they grow pale and thin, and turn green once they reach it. The turn is the bean's leaves pushing out of the hole into the sun. Underneath: a living thing that keeps reaching for the light, slowly, and a child who learns to do the same.
ask: How did the bean find the hole when it had no eyes?
Why was the stem pale inside the box, and the leaves green outside?
How was Meera like the bean?
What does Nani mean when she says 'Hm'?
Can you think of a time you kept trying, slowly, like the bean?

ideas.idea: Plants are alive and they act.
ideas.more: They drink, make food, grow towards light and away from gravity, and make seeds. They do it slowly, so we don't notice. A time-lapse video shows plants moving all day.
A leaf turns sunlight, water and air into food. Almost all the food on Earth, including ours, starts this way.
Plants have special proteins that sense light and even its colour, so they can tell the difference between sunlight and the shade of another leaf.
Turn a sprouting seed upside down and its root turns round to grow down again. Roots feel gravity and grow towards it; shoots grow away from it.

unknowns: Do plants feel anything when they are cut or eaten? They send electrical signals, but whether there is any 'feeling' is not known.
Plants can tell the colour of light and even 'remember' how long the nights have been. Scientists still don't fully understand how a plant without a brain keeps track of time.
How does a root tip decide where to go when it meets a stone, a worm or another root? Scientists can see roots turning, but the whole story of how they 'choose' is not known yet.

check.q: Show me the root, stem, leaf and flower.
check.a: Points correctly on a real plant.
It makes the plant's food from sunlight, water and air.

check.q: How does water get from the roots to the leaves?

check.q: Which way does a plant on a windowsill lean? Why?
check.a: Towards the window, because it grows towards light.

check.q: What did the roots do when we turned the jar upside down?
check.a: They turned round and grew down again, because roots feel gravity.

check.q: What happened to the moong in the dark?
check.a: It grew tall, thin and yellow, looking for light; it can't make its green without light.

check.q: Name one thing we eat that is a root, one that is a leaf and one that is a seed.
check.a: For example: carrot (root), spinach (leaf), dal or rice (seed).

check.q: Is a plant alive? How do you know?
check.a: Yes: it grows, drinks, makes food, responds to light and gravity, and makes seeds.
